description.narrative: # of in-country partners self-reporting improved participation in programming and policy-making at local, national, regional and/or global levels
# of in-country partners self-reporting improved participation in programming and policy-making at local, national, regional and/or global levels

comment.narrative:
In total 7 in country partners report improved participation in programming and policy making. The in-country partners IFRAD, PALM corps, GNH, UCOBAC, USSIA, Tunado and SSURA show improvement in their ability to participate in programming and policy making. For this reporting period, the ability to bring the voices of the affected population into the response is not taken into account, as this is not taken into account in the baseline score. Next year we will report on the progress related to the score in this report.
The findings across coordination, policy influence, programming influence, and community‑voice integration illustrate both the commitment and the constraints experienced by the 12 in‑country partners. The overall picture shows strong engagement and clear contributions at multiple levels, yet also highlights that the ability to structurally influence decision‑making spaces—whether coordination mechanisms, policy processes, or programming priorities—remains limited to only a few organisations. Resource constraints, insufficient access to higher‑level platforms, and the dominance of larger actors continue to affect how consistently partners can participate and shape outcomes. At the same time, the examples provided show meaningful progress: partners are driving change in areas such as land rights, education, livelihoods, and community feedback systems, often with targeted support yielding immediate improvements.
A key reflection emerging from the assessment process itself is the importance of jointly conducting the partner assessment in a face‑to‑face meeting. While responsibility for completing the self‑assessment was given to partners, the results indicate that additional clarification, shared interpretation of the questions, and mutual discussion of scoring criteria would significantly enhance data quality. Partners also expressed that such in‑person guidance is valuable, ensuring a shared understanding of concepts such as “structural influence,” “meaningful participation,” and “policy engagement.” Moving forward, conducting the assessment together—rather than remotely—will not only strengthen consistency and reliability of the data but also deepen dialogue, learning, and ownership of the capacity‑strengthening agenda.
Participation in Coordination Mechanisms Across the 12 in‑country partners, 10 are part of at least one coordination mechanism, and 8 of them participate often or always, demonstrating strong engagement in local and national platforms. However, only 4 partners report being able to structurally and meaningfully influence these mechanisms, while 7 say they can contribute sometimes, indicating that only a minority can consistently shape coordination outcomes and that there is still clear room for improvement. Overall capacity to participate is mixed: 7 partners rate their capacity as good or very good, 2 find it acceptable, and 1 rates it as poor. The biggest challenges relate to limited resources—especially staffing, time, and funding—which restrict consistent attendance and follow-up across the many coordination platforms operating simultaneously at district and settlement levels. As CEFORD explained: “First, resource limitations particularly staffing and time sometimes restrict consistent attendance and follow-up across multiple coordination platforms… Secondly, information flow and feedback loops are not always timely.” Additional barriers include slow information flow, limited access to higher‑level policy spaces, bureaucratic data systems, and the pressure to respond to unfunded priorities expected by actors such as UNHCR and OPM.”
Despite these constraints, partners continue to contribute actively through livelihood working groups, advocacy for land access and education rights, and participation in community-level events—for example through value‑addition demonstrations during World Refugee Day. Two partners requested support to strengthen their advocacy and to be introduced into refugee governance committees; while this targeted support was delivered satisfactorily, only for one organization this already led to improved ability to structurally influence coordination mechanisms, for the strengthening the advocacy capacity a follow-up is needed.
Ability to Influence Policies Across the partnership, 6 out of 12 organisations have been able to meaningfully contribute to policy development over the past year, engaging in stakeholder consultations, technical working groups, and community‑level processes. Their contributions include influencing local and national policies such as the education ordinance in Yumbe, women’s land rights, the Marriage Bill, National Land Policy, IGAD Gender Strategy, and the National Land Act, as well as sectoral contributions like TUNADO’s role in the national agroforestry strategy and hosting the All Africa Apimondia Symposium. Despite this engagement, only 2 out of 12 organisations report being able to consistently and structurally influence policy—typically those with strong technical roles, national mandates, or working‑group memberships—while 4 others can influence only occasionally due to limited access to national forums, resource and staffing constraints, policy‑analysis capacity gaps, and the dominance of larger actors in decision‑making spaces. Importantly, only 2 organisations explicitly requested support for policy engagement (in livelihoods and advocacy/policy training), and this support is not yet provided according to the request, so follow-up is needed.
Ability to Influence Programming Across the partnership, 7 out of 12 organisations report being able to meaningfully contribute to contextualising humanitarian programming standards at local, national, or regional level. They do so by engaging in settlement‑level sector planning, national NGO networks, and regional platforms such as C4C, IGAD, and Apimondia, contributing to areas like livelihoods and nutrition planning, localisation commitments, governance strengthening, and sector‑specific standards such as honey quality and apiculture policy. Examples include COW Foundation’s role in developing the livelihoods and nutrition sector plan in Palabek, and TUNADO’s influence in securing the recognition of honey as a strategic national commodity and strengthening apiculture extension services.
In addition, 6 partners have influenced in‑country programme priorities—such as developing the West Nile horticulture strategy, promoting beekeeping as a livelihood priority, and shaping INGOs’ programming directions (e.g., “we successfully engaged with AWO International to prioritize migration and land governance… and influenced Light For The World to incorporate gender programming”). 5 out of 12 partners were also able to influence donor priorities, contributing to programme design processes, advocating for inclusion of vulnerable groups, and aligning interventions with locally identified needs. However, this influence remains constrained by donors’ fixed priorities, earmarked funding, limited access to high‑level design spaces, and shrinking resource envelopes, which particularly affect smaller organisations.
Only one partner is able to structurally and consistently influence programming by international partners, largely due to holding a national apex position with recognised technical expertise. Seven others are sometimes able to influence programming through evidence sharing, consultation forums, and joint planning, but are limited by financial constraints, lack of access to international donor platforms, and power imbalances that favour larger INGOs. As CEFORD notes, there is a strong need for “networking and linkages especially with international donors through convening which we encourage Woord en Daad to champion.”
Finally, only 2 out of 12 partners explicitly requested support to strengthen their ability to influence programming—one on programming influence in general and one on specialised capacity building from another international organisation. Neither request has yet been addressed according to the self-reporting sheet so there is a need to follow-up.
Ability to Bring the Voices of Affected Populations Into Responses Most partners have strengthened their ability to bring community voices into programming: 7 out of 12 improved access to information through community meetings, sensitisation, and clear communication on programme objectives; 9 out of 12 enhanced active involvement by using participatory needs assessments, community dialogues, and joint decision‑making; and 11 out of 12 strengthened feedback systems through channels such as community meetings, suggestion boxes, WhatsApp lines, digital tools like DamuBox, and trained CFRM structures. While 4 organisations can structurally ensure community voices are represented (and 3 can do so sometimes), their efforts are often constrained by resource limitations, coordination challenges, bureaucratic systems, and contextual issues such as land scarcity and tensions between refugees and host communities. Seven partners explicitly requested support—mainly in communication, advocacy, MEAL/MIS, financial management, and documentation—and 4 received timely and tailored assistance, which they report has directly strengthened their capacity. For example, HDF noted that “Communication expert was deployed… HDF staff communicate better to various stakeholders,” while GNH highlighted how MIS and MEAL support now enables them to systematically collect and integrate community feedback into programme adjustments.

comment.narrative: Across the programme, in‑country partners reported a substantial number of successful efforts to influence policies and programming at different levels. In total, partners documented 6 instances of contributing to policy development, demonstrating their growing ability to engage in and shape policy processes. They also reported some cases where they played a role in contextualising humanitarian programming standards at local, national, or regional levels, ensuring that responses are better aligned with the realities of the communities they serve. In addition, partners highlighted a few instances where they contributed to in‑country priorities, including programme design and implementation by international actors such as INGOs and UN agencies. Together, these instances reflect a clear and expanding capacity among partners to effectively influence programming and policy across multiple levels, of which mainly the influence on policy development was well documented with clear impact.

comment.narrative:
Across the 12 participating incountry partners, 10 explicitly requested capacity strengthening, spanning anywhere from a single thematic area to all seven capacity domains defined in the LEAD approach. Analysis of reported results shows that six partners selfreported increased capacity across three or more key areas, demonstrating significant progress toward their selfidentified objectives. These improvements were particularly evident in financial management, MEAL systems, governance, and core programming. The adoption of tools such as QuickBooks Online enabled realtime financial reporting and improved documentation, while use of Solstice MIS and other upgraded MEAL systems enhanced partners’ ability to collect, analyze, and use data for decisionmaking. Investments in infrastructure, such as solar systems, further improved operational reliability and productivity, contributing to stronger program delivery.
Capacity strengthening also contributed to organizational development, with six organizations updating or developing key policies and guidelines, including human resource, safeguarding/PSEA, finance, overhead, data management, advocacy and communication, accounting, procurement manuals, and strategic plans. These institutional changes demonstrate that partners not only applied the new competencies but integrated them into longterm systems and structures. The qualitative feedback from partners reinforces this progress. As shared by incountry partner HDF: “In policy influencing, our capacity to be able to execute community barazas, an activity which involves engaging several stakeholders, has been strengthened. HDF is now an endorser to Charter 4 Change, and is also pursuing membership in several networks. In other projects, HDF is speaking with key stakeholders on policies related to Sexual and Reproductive Health, and it is because the trainings on Gender, and policy influencing have been very key to our growth.” Similarly, GNH reported that: “Finance systems have been Set and enhanced by the SP. M&E systems have been enhanced and made user friendly. The engagement of GNH leaders into Board trainings by WD has strengthened our management systems by Conducting (TOT)” —both examples illustrating increased capacity across multiple areas.
Satisfaction levels were correspondingly high, with 83% of partners reporting being satisfied or very satisfied with the capacity building received. Those who responded highlighted that the support was welltailored to their needs and core mission and delivered respectfully. Only 29% mentioned that the duration of support was insufficient, though it was not clarified whether it was too short or too long. Despite the overall positive experience, partners identified several opportunities for strengthening future capacity development. Common suggestions included establishing more regular support cycles (quarterly or annual), reinforcing MEAL systems through staffing, refresher training, improved tools, and system refinements, and enhancing HR systems and sustainability capacities such as fundraising and strategic influence. The importance of shared learning was emphasized, as noted by incountry partner UCOBAC: “Establishing on-line knowledge hubs and more peer-learning sessions for partners to learn, share experiences and best practices would help them work more effectively and maximize overall impact of the LEAD program.”
Overall, the evidence shows that most in‑country partners not only received targeted capacity strengthening but also successfully increased their capacity across multiple key areas, contributing meaningfully to progress toward indicator 1.1. As a next step, the support partner will follow up with each organization to review how their capacity has grown over the past year and update their organizational capacity‑building plans, since the full target has not yet been reached. This process will help ensure that emerging needs are addressed alongside the capacity development already underway. In addition, several case studies documenting best practices have been collected, offering a strong foundation for developing learning hubs and fostering peer‑to‑peer exchange.

comment.narrative: Across the LEAD programme, a large number of participants accessed formal or informal education and training courses. The majority of those trained (61%) were refugees, while a substantial share (39%) came from host communities. Overall satisfaction with the education and training services was high: 85% of participants reported that the services were delivered in a safe, accessible, accountable, and participatory manner. In addition, 84% of respondents were able to access feedback and complaint mechanisms, indicating that training and service‑delivery structures were well established and reachable. Altogether, the results reflect high participation and strong positive outcomes from the programme’s education and training components.

comment.narrative:
83% of partners (10 out of 12 partners) say that the funding provided is partner adequate to deliver programmatic response that meets quality standards and commitments agreed in the funding contract. This means two in-country partners score the funding as insufficient, because of overwhelming demand for services and the funds are not sufficient to cover all needs of the communities. That is not related to the quality of funding, but on the quantity. The majority of in-country partners state that the funding was in line with the budget that they themselves developed, for example In-country partner Palm Corps: The budget was fully developed by us (ICP) and there is great level of flexibility demonstrating trust and mutual respect. Although a number of them also mention that the needs of the community are higher, for example In-country partner CEFORD: However, while the available resources have sufficiently supported the agreed outputs, the scale and complexity of needs within the target communities remain significantly higher.
On average, 8.2% of partner funding is classified as ICR/overhead, with values ranging from 6–10%. All partners receive multi annual funding, and although two indicated otherwise, these were confirmed as reporting mistakes. Only 10 partners stated they receive overhead without conditions, in the self-reporting tool, but during the MEL session was confirmed that all partners received overhead funding without reporting conditions. About 66% (8/12) report that they are informed about the support partner’s budgeting and funding situation. The partnership is described as financially transparent, with budgets, allocations, and cost allowability shared openly, co creation meetings, and Steering Committee participation strengthening collaboration—most remarks refer to transparency around in country budgets. As one in country partner noted: “The IFRAD Executive Director sits on the LEAD project Steering Committee meetings alongside other organizational Executives and Woord en Daad staff. This is a platform where project decisions are made and such information is shared.”
Regarding financial flexibility, 91% (11/12) said reasonable budget adjustments were possible, usually one time reallocations due to changing conditions or prices. Furthermore, 75% (9/12) confirmed that the funding contracts contribute to preparedness, stability, and quality. The multi year commitments allow organizations to plan ahead, retain staff, and maintain operational continuity, while capacity building elements—such as finance, MEAL, MIS, digital tools, and organizational strengthening—reinforce readiness and improve programme quality. As one partner (CEFORD) emphasized: “1) The support partner has guaranteed operations for at least 4 years with yearly contracts; 2) the support partner is building our capacity in the areas that are most needed… All the above are helping to maintain stability and preparedness and deepening the quality of our programming overtime.”
Finally, 58% of partners (7 out of 12) reported that the support partner was approachable and responsive regarding issues related to qualitative funding. This point was further discussed during the MEL session, where partners indicated that in future it would be beneficial to address such questions face‑to‑face to ensure clearer communication and mutual understanding.

description.narrative: 1 OidR programming contributed to the improved access of FDPs and HCMs to (decent) jobs, entrepreneurship and income-generating activities
1 OidR programming contributed to the improved access of FDPs and HCMs to (decent) jobs, entrepreneurship and income-generating activities

comment.narrative:
A total of 912 participants (51%) successfully started their own business or income generating activity, and almost all of them — 849 participants (94%) — are already earning a regular income from these activities. This demonstrates that the vast majority of supported enterprises are not only operational but also delivering meaningful economic benefits to participants.
Beyond entrepreneurship, the programme supported a large group of participants in accessing wage employment after completing their training: 46% of all traced individuals were able to secure a paid job. However, the nature of this employment reflects the realities of the refugee context, where people often combine multiple livelihood strategies. A significant share of the employment obtained was parttime (32%) or temporary (24%), while 43% accessed fulltime work. Only 178 participants were able to maintain stable wage employment over a longer period, mainly due to the delayed start of interventions and the limited availability of longterm job opportunities. These patterns show that while the programme was effective in enabling people to enter the labour market and diversify their income sources, structural barriers continue to limit access to sustained, stable employment.
In total, 1,202 trained participants engaged in some form of economic activity (either wage employment, income generation or both). A notable pattern is that 526 individuals combined wage employment with income generating activities, reflecting the typical livelihood strategies in refugee contexts where people diversify income sources to manage economic uncertainty and reduce risk.
These livelihood outcomes translated into strong improvements at household level. Across the programme, 80% of all traced households report being able to meet their basic needs — slightly higher among host communities (84%) than refugees (77%), though with weaker outcomes in certain districts such as Kyegegwa (37%) and Lamwo (32%). Income trends reinforce this positive picture: 88% of participants experienced an increase in household income, and 42% achieved an increase of more than 20% compared to baseline. Together, these results show that the programme’s combined support for entrepreneurship, diversified livelihoods, and employment has significantly contributed to improved economic wellbeing for both refugees and host community members.
